title: Maths reference: Data and chance
summary: The words and methods from Data and chance, each with an example and, where it helps, a picture of the board.
_about: Maths cards for maths/data (see snippets/maths.json for the format).

items.label: discrete and continuous
items.hint: Discrete data takes separate values (number of siblings). Continuous data can be any value in a range (height, time), and is rounded when recorded.

items.label: mean
items.hint: Add the values, then share equally. An outlier pulls the mean towards it.
items.board:
widget: data
values: 3, 5, 5, 6, 11
range: 0, 15
show: mean, median

items.label: median
items.hint: Sort first; the middle value, or halfway between the two middle values for an even count.

items.label: mode and range
items.hint: There can be two modes, or none. The range is a simple measure of spread.

items.label: choosing a measure
items.hint: With an outlier, the median describes a typical value better than the mean. Without, the mean uses every value. For 'most common', use the mode.

items.label: stem-and-leaf plot
items.hint: Tens as stems, units as leaves in order; include every stem, even with no leaves; give a key.
items.board:
widget: data
values: 23, 31, 35, 35, 38, 42, 47, 51
view: stem
show: none
items.shows: Stems are the tens, leaves the units

items.label: comparing data sets
items.hint: Describe shape (symmetrical or skewed, clusters, gaps, outliers), centre and spread. Compare both centre and spread, with numbers, in context.
items.board:
widget: data
values: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 17, 18
second: 6, 10, 13, 16, 19, 20, 22
names: Class A, Class B
range: 0, 25
show: median, range
items.shows: Similar medians; Class B much more spread

items.label: statistical investigation
items.hint: Ask a question data can answer, plan the variable and a fair sample, collect and display the data, describe its shape, centre and spread, then report the answer with its limits.

items.label: sample space
items.hint: Every possible outcome, listed once. Check whether the outcomes are equally likely.

items.label: probability
items.hint: For equally likely outcomes. Otherwise use sizes or counts. From 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain); all outcomes add to 1.
items.board:
widget: chance
device: spinner
outcomes: red 2, blue 1, green 1
watch: blue
seed: 4
items.shows: A half-red spinner: P(red) = 1/2, P(blue) = P(green) = 1/4

items.label: expected count
items.hint: Expected count = probability × trials. Real results vary around it, more so in short experiments.

items.label: relative frequency
items.hint: The experiment's estimate of the probability. Over many trials it settles close to the probability (the law of large numbers); nothing is ever 'due'.
items.board:
widget: chance
device: coin
seed: 2
start: 2000
items.shows: 2000 flips: the relative frequency of heads settles near 0.5

items.label: complementary events
items.hint: An event and its complement cover every outcome once. For 'at least one', count the outcomes with none and subtract from 1.
items.board:
widget: events
first: dice
event: a >= 5
complement: shown
items.shows: Roll 5 or 6 (A) and the other four outcomes (not A)

items.label: Venn diagram and two-way table
items.hint: Two yes/no properties make four groups: one only, both, the other only, neither. Each is a region of the Venn diagram and a cell of the table.
items.board:
widget: venn
labels: Sport, Music
counts: 12, 8, 5, 5
items.shows: The same 30 students as a Venn diagram and a two-way table

items.label: grid and tree diagram
items.hint: Two events make pairs: a grid or a tree lists every pair once, and the number of outcomes is the two counts multiplied. HT and TH are different outcomes.
items.board:
widget: events
first: red, blue, green
second: coin
names: Spinner, Coin
view: tree
event: b = H
items.shows: A spinner with three equal parts, then a coin: 6 outcomes, 3 of them heads

items.label: and, or, not
items.code: P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \text{ and } B)
items.hint: And is the overlap; or is one, the other or both; not A is everything outside A. Count each outcome once.
items.board:
widget: venn
labels: Dog, Cat
counts: 9, 4, 6, 11
event: a or b
items.shows: Dog or cat: everything inside the circles, 19 of 30

items.label: simulation
items.hint: Run many trials with random numbers (=RANDBETWEEN(1,6) is a dice) and compare the relative frequency with the probability. Short runs can be well off.
items.board:
widget: events
first: dice
second: dice
show: sum
event: s >= 10
items.shows: Two dice with a total of 10 or more chosen (6 of 36), ready to simulate

items.label: census and sample
items.hint: A census is exact but slow and costly; a sample estimates. An experiment changes something on purpose; an observation watches.
items.board:
widget: sample
measure: sleep
method: random
n: 20
seed: 4
start: 1
items.shows: A random sample of 20 from a school of 200

items.label: bias
items.hint: Bias pushes a result one way: sampling bias (who is asked), response bias (how they are asked), measurement bias (the tool). A bigger sample doesn't fix it.
items.board:
widget: sample
measure: sport
method: convenience
n: 20
seed: 6
start: 1
items.shows: A convenience sample: all from Year 7, pushed high

items.label: sampling methods
items.hint: Simple random: same chance for all. Systematic: every kth from a random start. Stratified: at random within each group, in proportion. Convenience and quota: someone chooses, so they can be biased.

items.label: describing a sample
items.hint: Describe the shape (symmetric or skewed), the centre (mean, median) and the spread (range), then estimate the population with the method and size. Primary data you collect; secondary data others collected.
items.board:
widget: sample
measure: sleep
method: random
n: 40
plot: values
seed: 11
start: 1
items.shows: A random sample of 40 students' sleep as a dot plot

items.label: sampling variation
items.hint: Fair samples from one population give different results by chance. Their results scatter around the population's value, closer for bigger samples.
items.board:
widget: sample
measure: sport
method: random
n: 20
seed: 5
start: 20
items.shows: 20 samples of 20: results scattered around the school's value

items.label: inference
items.code: \text{about } \ldots \text{, from a random sample of } n
items.hint: Infer only about the population sampled, give an estimate, and say how sure you are (size and method). Collect data with consent and anonymity.
